title: A Man with No Clock
passages:
The rig's engine cut without a cough, the sudden silence heavy after the long grade. Orlin Dray let the brake settle, felt the chassis sigh into its springs, and climbed down into air that tasted of cold ore dust and old grease. His hand lamp hit the dirt with a dull thunk, its beam pooling yellow across the plate steel bolted to the threshold — C9 cut deep, fresh as a wound.

Forty meters ahead, the receiving jaw gaped around the blank rig. Its hand lamp still burned in the crew box, a small stubborn flame behind the grate. Eleven canisters sat locked in the clamp, logged now under Culvert Nine's mark by a reader no one had touched in seasons.

Saul stood at the door plate's edge, clipboard braced against his hip, pencil bitten flat at the end. He didn't reach for his sidearm. He didn't step forward. His eyes tracked Dray's rig — no transponder, no board, plates welded over with yard steel — then flicked to the lamp on the ground, the way a man notes a landmark.

"Marrow Cut," Saul said. Not a question.

"Spur master Dray." Dray wiped his palms on his thighs, the motion slow, deliberate. "The rig in your jaw came off my yard. Two names short on its plate. I'm here to collect it."

Saul's pencil moved. Scratch of graphite. "Logged as Anza salvage. No living names wired. Blank plate."

Dray gestured at the lamp between them, the blank rig, the grade stretching north. "I've got fuel for three weeks and no schedule that says I leave. I'll wait as long as my fuel holds."

Saul tucked the clipboard under his arm and walked the forty meters to the jaw. The grate still held eleven canisters, their steel lids stamped with numbers he couldn't read from this distance. He keyed his handheld reader against the crew-box plate welded over with yard steel. The screen blinked once, then held: ANZA SALVAGE. NO LIVING NAMES WIRED. CLAIM PENDING.

He walked back to the door plate. Odessa Brill had come out while he was gone. She stood in the opening with the steel crank in her fist, her coat belted tight against the ore dust, her breath coming in short white clouds.

"The plate reads Anza salvage," Saul said. "No living names wired to it."

Brill didn't lower the crank. "Then whose ghost rig is it sitting in my jaw?"

"Dray says it's his."

"He doesn't cross my plate. He doesn't wire names. He sits out there with his lamp and his fuel and waits." She stepped closer, keeping the crank between them. "I want those ten canisters unloaded before the jaw trips again. Before the spoiled one ruins the batch. Ten good cans. That's my price."

"Anza salvage isn't yours to price," Saul said.

"It's sitting in my jaw. My reader woke this morning and logged it into Kettering's queue. My door plate says C9." She tapped the crank against her thigh. "You want it moved, you pay the crank. You don't pay, it stays locked. And if it stays locked past oh-eight-hundred, I call Kettering and tell them their salvage is walking off my board before their desk even opens. Let them sort the claim with Dray while my crew eats the spoiled can."

Dray's hand lamp still burned on the dirt between the two rigs, small and stubborn. He had not moved from his running board.

Brill looked past Saul at the yellow pool, then back at Saul. "He's not leaving. I can see that. So either you open the jaw, or I make the call."

Something had shifted between them. She was no longer asking Saul to move a rig; she was naming the hour when she would go over his head entirely.

Brill came out to the edge of her door plate and stopped with her boots on the steel, forty meters of ore dirt between her and Dray's running board, his lamp burning in the middle of it like something set down and forgotten.

"I'll trade," she called. "That's all this is. You want the rig, you haul it off my jaw and the cans go with it. Ten good and the spoiled one in the same clamp. I don't crack a seal, I don't call Kettering, and my reader logs it out claimed instead of salvaged." She lifted the crank so the lamplight ran along it. "And the crank. Only one that fits the jaw pin. You'll want it, hauling heavy."

Dray didn't get off the running board. He looked at the crank the way a man looks at a wrench he already owns.

"Can for cans," he said. "You're selling me my own rig and calling it a trade."

"I'm selling you eleven cans and a crank."

"I've got cans in my shed and a crank on my wall." He shifted his weight, and the running board took it with a groan. "You want to trade, trade something that's yours."

"Everything in that jaw is mine till oh-eight-hundred. That's what the reader says."

"The reader says salvage." Dray tipped his chin at the jaw. "Salvage is a word for a thing nobody's using. There's a crew plate on that box, welded over with yard steel, and there's two staples in it with no wire through them. Two names short. You put a living name on that plate, wired and witnessed, and what's in your jaw stops being salvage and starts being a rig with a crew in it. No names, no crew. No crew, it's a parts pile, and I don't haul parts piles. I haul rigs."

"Then wire it yourself. You've got a whole yard."

"I buy names," Dray said. "I don't make them."

Brill's laugh came out short and cold. "You drove down the ore line for a name."

"Two of them."

"Names." She said it like a bad weld. "I've got a board in there with names on it. Half of them's pencil. I can write you out anything you want and Saul will witness it, he loves a pencil."

"Written isn't wired." Dray reached down and picked up his lamp, and the pool of yellow slid off the plate steel and up her coat. "Wired, witnessed, before that jaw turns again. That's my price. It doesn't move and I don't come across your plate to collect it."

"Everything has a price that moves."

"Not this one."

The wind came down off the grade and moved the ore dust in low sheets. Behind Brill, in the storeroom doorway, Miko stood with the manifest sheet against her chest and didn't say anything, which for Miko was practically a religious experience.

Brill looked at the blank rig's crew box, at the small stubborn flame behind the grate, and then at the clamp holding eleven cans she could not feed her people if she handed over. Her thumb worked the crank's grip.

"Two names," she said. "Any two?"

"Any two that'll stand up and answer to them."

"There's nine people under this roof and every one of them eats out of my storeroom." She set the crank's heel on the plate steel. "You'd take two of them off my tally and drive north with them wired to a box, and I'd still have a jaw full of cans I can't touch. That's not a trade, Dray. That's a bill."

"It's a price," Dray said. "You've got till the jaw trips."

Behind her, in the dark of the storeroom, somebody set a crate down very quietly, the way you do when you'd rather not be counted.

Saul turned the clipboard over. On the back, under a header stained with old grease, was Marrow Cut's book. He ran his thumb down the first page.

"A rig lives while a living name is wired to its crew plate," Saul said, his voice flat. "No name wired, no movement. A rig brought in blank is a parts pile until a name stands behind it."

Brill's grip on the crank didn't loosen, but her shoulders tightened like she'd just taken a step she hadn't meant to.

"You read that like scripture," she said.

"It's the yard's rule," Saul said. "Dray didn't drive down the ore line for diesel. He's not haggling over fuel. He's buying bodies."

Dray said nothing from his running board. He held his lamp steady, the beam pooling yellow across the door plate steel.

Brill looked from Saul to the blank rig's crew box, where the small flame still burned behind the grate. Eleven canisters in the clamp. Her storeroom behind her was full of cans she couldn't open without a trade and now couldn't justify without a name.

"So that's it," she said. "You want two of my people wired to your plate so your rig stops being salvage and starts being yours. You came down here to buy crew."

"I came to collect my rig," Dray said. "It's two names short. You've got nine under this roof. Do the math."

"I'm not running a labor auction out of my door plate," Brill snapped. "My crew isn't your currency."

"Then it stays a parts pile," Dray said. "And the jaw stays closed."

The wind pushed ore dust across the plate steel. Miko stayed in the storeroom doorway, the manifest sheet against her chest, saying nothing. Whoever had set the crate down had gone quiet again, as if they'd heard enough.

Brill shifted her weight, the crank braced between them. She looked at the canisters, at Saul's reader, at Dray's lamp burning between two rigs on a grade with no schedule.

"You're not buying fuel," she said quietly. "You're buying bodies."

Dray nodded once. "Two names. Wired. Witnessed. Before oh-eight-hundred, or nothing moves."

"I'll call Kettering," she said.

Saul lifted his reader. "My queue already logged it as Anza salvage with no living names wired. You call them, they'll see two names short and mark it derelict before oh-eight-hundred even opens. Then it's not your salvage anymore. It's Kettering's scrap."

The crank felt heavy in Brill's fist. She had nine names on her board, half in pencil, and a storeroom full of winter she couldn't feed if she gave two away—and couldn't feed if she didn't.

"Two names," Dray said. "Or sit there with your jaw full of cans you can't touch and your board full of names you can't spare."

Brill let the crank swing down until its heel rang on the plate steel.

"Mine, then," she said. "Take mine. One name off my board and one body in your cab, and you haul your rig out of my jaw with the cans still in the clamp. That's a trade with something in it that's actually mine."

Dray didn't get off the running board. "Say it again."

"You heard me."

"I heard noise." He set his lamp on the dirt a second time, beam up, so the light lay across her boots. "A name spoken twice in front of a witness is a thing I can cut. You want it in my book, stand on your own steel and say it like you mean to be written down."

"Odessa Brill." Her voice carried flat down the grade. "Wired, witnessed, whatever your word is. Saul heard it."

Saul turned the clipboard around, thumb on the greased header. "Rule says a name cut in a plate belongs to the plate. Yours is cut in that door steel, C9 beside it, and your mark's under it on Anza's board in front of two shifts. One name, one plate. Wire it twice, the wire holds nothing."

"So cut it out of the door."

"Cut your name out of that steel and the jaw loses its mark." Saul didn't look up. "Reader drops the clamp to unclaimed, my queue sends it to Kettering as scrap before oh-eight-hundred, and you've got nothing in the jaw to sell anybody."

"Half a plate," Dray said. "I'm two names short. One name closes half of nothing."

"It closes a hell of a lot of my winter," Brill said.

"Your name's too good." Dray picked at something on his glove. "It's spent. It's in a door and a tally and a board three nodes down. I don't haul stations. I haul crew. The bargain I came down this line for was two living names wired to a box, and you're offering me the only hand that fits that crank. That's not the letter of it."

"The letter of it." Brill laughed, one short crack of it. "You'd let a rig rot to a parts pile over how a sentence was said."

"I'd let it rot over a name that isn't there."

Miko shifted in the storeroom doorway, manifest still flat against her chest. "He's got a point about the crank. Who turns it if she's north?"

"Nobody asked the loader," Brill said, without turning around.

"Nobody ever does. That's how you end up with a board in pencil."

Brill's jaw worked. She looked back into the dark of the storeroom, where nine people were being very quiet about being nine people, and then at the eleven cans sitting in the clamp with the yard's little flame burning behind the grate over them.

"Fine. Not mine. Pick one off my board and I'll call them out to stand on the steel."

"You call them," Dray said. "They walk out here on their own boots and say it with their own mouth. A name in a book isn't a name on a plate. I don't take what's handed to me over a threshold."

"You take two cans off me and give nothing back."

"I take a trade. I don't take a gift." He tipped his chin at the jaw. "Gift's got no witnesses worth the name."

Out at the jaw, the clamp ticked — one small metal sound, the kind a cold rig makes when it settles onto its pins. Then it ticked again, and a thin line of wet showed along the lid of the third can from the left, where the spoiled one sat sweating in the cold.

Saul lifted his reader and read the screen. "Clamp's got maybe ninety minutes before it faults and calls it derelict on its own."

"Then you'd better start walking people out to the steel," Dray said.

"I don't have two people to walk," Brill said. "I've got nine and a storeroom and a jaw I can't turn, and you sitting on a running board with no clock on you at all."

"Never needed one." Dray settled back against the cab. "The fuel's the clock."

Brill turned her head without taking her eyes off the lamp. "Ardo. Pike. Somebody come stand on the steel."

The storeroom gave her nothing. Then, out of the dark, the small sound of a crate set down and picked up again — somebody deciding, in real time, that they were busy elsewhere.

"They heard you," Saul said.

"They hear that stove every night when it's lit."

"Then say a name."

"I'm not calling a name out to be cut off my roster in front of a yard man." She shifted the crank to her other hand. "You want a body, Dray, come across and take one. That's what you do, isn't it. Buy and haul."

"I don't cross a plate I haven't been given leave to cross," Dray said. "And you haven't given me leave. You've given me a price."

"It's the same road."

"It's a different road with a fence on it." He hitched himself up onto the running board, boots hanging, lamp burning at his heel. "A name said inside a doorway is said under a roof that feeds the mouth saying it. That's not a name, that's a man talking about somebody. I need it said out here on steel with the sky on it and two people hearing it who don't eat out of your pot."

"So the plate stays shut."

"The plate stays shut till the second name goes in my book." He said it the way a man reads a number off a gauge. "Then I'll come across, take that crank out of your fist, turn your pin myself, and haul my rig north with the cans still in the clamp. Not one minute before."

Saul lifted his reader, thumbed the screen, and read it out flat. "Eighty-six minutes. Clamp faults on its own, marks derelict, my queue sends it up to Kettering as scrap, and the desk at oh-eight-hundred does what desks do with scrap."

Brill looked at the jaw. The third can from the left had sweated a thin bright line down its flank, and a drop had gathered on the clamp pin and hung there, in no hurry.

"Ten good cans," she said. "Nine people. That's thirty-one days if I'm careful, and I'm never careful, I'm just loud about it. You want two of my nine to hand me back eleven I already own." She let out a breath. "That's the worst exchange rate on the Interior and I've bought water at Ospina."

"I'm not selling," Dray said. "You are."

"I've got a claim. Reader says Anza salvage, reader says C9, and there's C9 cut in my door with a hand's width of steel around it. That's mine."

"It's a claim on a parts pile. Nobody's ever eaten a claim."

"Then you'll sit out here three weeks and I'll sit in there three weeks, and one of us has a stove."

"I've got a stove," Dray said. "It's just up the line."

That landed. She didn't answer it, which for Brill was practically a confession.

Miko leaned out of the doorway with the manifest still flat against her chest. "For the record, whoever turns that crank has to be standing here when it turns. So it's not two names you're short, it's two names and a hand, and the hand's already spoken for."

"Nobody asked the loader," Brill said.

"Nobody ever does."

Dray reached inside his coat and came out with a book, small and swollen with damp, and did not open it. "Odessa. One more thing, since we're both going to be here a while. Your reader woke this morning on a wire nobody at Culvert Nine cut. That wire's been spliced into the ore line's queue since before the frost, and my yard's board hears everything that runs that queue. Ten good, one spoiled, eleven received C9, blank rig, Anza salvage. I knew your count before I came past the second culvert."

Saul's pencil stopped.

"So I didn't drive down here for your cans," Dray said. "I came for my rig, and I came because somebody has been reading your jaw out loud for a year and a half, and I would like to know who before they get around to reading my shed."
